sentiment.instructions: Judge the overall sentiment or emotional tone the author expresses in the text (tweet-style, any language). Focus on the author's own attitude and feelings, including sarcasm and implied emotion, not just the topic mentioned.

positive.description: The author conveys happiness, excitement, anticipation, praise, gratitude, love, amusement, or good news (e.g., looking forward to an event, celebrating, offering an extra ticket to friends, admiring a performance or achievement, favorable outcomes).
examples: Not even 20 pages into Paper Towns and the book centers around the night of May 5th. I know its gonna be a good one now!

neutral.description: The text is mainly factual, informational, or a plain question/announcement (news headlines, schedules, sales listings, logistics, roleplay narration) with no clear emotional leaning, or with mixed/mild/joking tone that does not settle on either side.
examples: I may be sleep deprived but I promise you that some kid at Dunkin today looked like a sprout.

negative.description: The author conveys sadness, anger, frustration, disappointment, contempt, insults, threats, hostility, or complaint; or reports clearly bad events such as deaths, attacks, violence, or losses; includes sarcastic mockery, regret about missing something, and wishing harm on others.
examples: The tragedy of only thinking up hilarious tweets for the Summer Olympics now is that in four years there may be no place for them.
